title: Options and help pages
objectives: Change what a command does with options, and read its help.
Tell a command, its options and its arguments apart.
Know the two ways Windows PowerShell differs from the shell taught here.

screens.prose:
Here are two ways of listing the same folder. The second adds two characters, `-l`:

```sh
$ ls data
prices.csv  trades.csv
$ ls -l data
```

state.caption: The output of ls -l data, one line per file

screens.question: What did `-l` change?

options.text: Each file gets a long line of details: size, date and more

options.why: The same two files appear. Only the detail about each one changed.

options.text: `ls` showed what is inside the files
options.why: Reading a file's contents is a job for cat or head. ls only describes files.

options.text: `ls` showed the full path of each file
options.why: The names are the same short names. The path is what pwd prints.

hints.text: Compare the two outputs. Which files appear in each?
These columns are new.
The same two files, now with permissions, owner, size and date.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what each output shows about the same two files.

explain.text: The same two files appear, each with its size in bytes and the time it last changed. The dash and letter changed how ls behaves, not what it looks at. prices.csv is about five times the size of trades.csv.

screens.prose:
Another letter: `ls -t` sorts by the time each file last changed, newest first. Your trade exports folder holds four files.

```sh
$ ls -t
```

state.caption: Plain ls lists the names in alphabetical order.

screens.question: Tap the name `ls -t` prints first.

hints.text: Ignore the names and look at the times.
These two changed on 5 March. Which is later?

feedback.correct: trades_0305.csv changed last, at 18:01 on 5 March.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the latest time in the second column.

byKey.alpha: notes.txt is first in alphabetical order, and it changed on 5 March. But at 09:12, earlier than the 18:01 export.
byKey.oldest: That is the oldest file. ls -t puts the newest first.
byKey.r2c0: 4 March is newer than 1 March, but the 5 March export is newer still.

explain.text: ls -t ranks by time: trades_0305.csv, then notes.txt, then the 4 March and 1 March exports. The newest file comes first. That makes it easy to spot the latest export.

screens.prose:
`-l` and `-t` are **options**: a dash, then a letter that changes how a command behaves. Words without a dash are **arguments**: what the command works on. Some options take a value of their own:

```sh
$ head -n 3 prices.csv
```
screens.question: Drag each part of the command to its role.

hints.text: Which part starts with a dash?
head is the command, -n the option, 3 its value, and prices.csv the argument.

feedback.correct: Command, option, the option's value, then the argument.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The dash marks the option; the value follows it.

byKey.val: 3 belongs to -n: it says how many lines. The file is what head works on, so it is the argument.
byKey.arg: prices.csv is what head works on: the argument. The 3 is the value that -n needs.
byKey.opt: -n starts with a dash, so it is the option.
byKey.cmd: The command always comes first: head.

explain.text: head is the command, -n an option that takes a value, 3, and prices.csv the argument. Read it as: head, with 3 lines, on prices.csv. Every command line you have typed has this shape.

hints.text: head counts from the very first line.
The header is line 1.
Lines 1, 2 and 3: the header and two price rows.

feedback.correct: The header and the first two rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the first three lines, starting at the top.

byKey.skip-header: You skipped the header. head does not know it is special, so it counts as line 1.

explain.text: head -n 3 printed three lines, and the header used one of them. To see three price rows, ask for -n 4. head never treats a header differently from data.

screens.prose: Single-letter options can be written separately or squeezed behind one dash. You want the long listing, newest first.
screens.question: Which commands do the same as `ls -l -t`? Select all that apply.

options.why: Without a dash, lt is an argument. ls looks for a file called lt and reports it is missing.
The second dash sits inside one word. ls reads it as an option letter it does not know, and stops with an error.

hints.text: Does the order of the letters matter?
Letters behind one dash combine, in any order. A word with no dash is a name.

feedback.correct: Same two options, written three ways.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Letters can share one dash in any order; a word with no dash is a name.

explain.text: -lt, -tl and -t -l all switch on the same two options. The order of single letters does not matter here. Leaving out the dash turns the letters into a file name.

screens.prose:
Every command documents its options. `man sort` opens the manual for sort; press q to quit. Part of it reads:

```sh
-n    compare by numeric value
-r    reverse the result
```
screens.question: Which command prints the largest close first?

options.why: Without -n, sort compares text one character at a time. 99.10 would beat 102.30, because 9 comes after 1.
That sorts by value, smallest first. You also need -r to flip it.
That sorts as text, smallest first. 9.85 would come after 102.30.

hints.text: You need two things: compare as numbers, and flip the order.
As text, this line sorts before 102.30.
Use both options from the manual: -n and -r.

feedback.correct: -n compares values, -r puts the largest first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the manual: one option for numbers, one for reversing.

explain.text: sort -n -r prints 102.30, 100.40, 99.10, 9.85. Without -n, text order puts 9.85 above 102.30, because the character 9 beats 1. Reading two lines of the manual saved a wrong answer.

screens.prose:
On sort, `-r` means reverse. You have a folder, old_runs, full of last month's backtest results. You type:

```sh
$ rm -r old_runs
```
screens.question: What does this do?

options.text: Deletes the files in old_runs in reverse order
options.why: You carried -r over from sort. Each command defines its own letters; for rm, -r means recursive.

options.text: Deletes old_runs and everything inside it, with no undo

options.why: That would be -i, for interactive. -r asks nothing.
rm never restores anything, and the terminal has no Bin.

hints.text: Does a letter mean the same thing in every command?
For rm, -r means recursive: the folder and everything below it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what -r means for rm, not for sort.

byKey.reverse: You carried -r over from sort. Each command defines its own letters; for rm, -r means recursive.

explain.text: The same letter can mean different things in different commands: reverse for sort, recursive for rm and cp. Before an unfamiliar option, check `man` for that command. With rm, a wrong guess cannot be undone.

screens.prose: This course teaches the macOS and Linux shell. On Windows, PowerShell plays the terminal's role and knows `cd`, `ls` and `pwd`. Two differences matter. Paths use backslashes and a drive letter, as in `C:\Users\ana\data`. And Unix tools such as `grep` and `head`, with their one-letter options, are missing.
screens.question: Which line works unchanged in PowerShell?

options.why: PowerShell knows ls, but not its Unix option letters.
grep is one of the Unix tools PowerShell lacks.
head is one of the Unix tools PowerShell lacks.

hints.text: Which line uses no Unix tool and no option letters?
cd with a plain folder name works in both shells.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Avoid the Unix tools and the option letters.

explain.text: PowerShell moves around with the same cd, ls and pwd, but lacks grep, head and the option letters. On Windows, installing WSL or Git Bash gives you the exact commands in this course. Then everything here works unchanged.

screens.prose:
Every command line has the same shape: the command, then options, then arguments.

```sh
$ head -n 3 prices.csv
$ ls -lt ~/Downloads
$ man sort        # manual; q quits
$ ls --help        # short help, Linux
$ python3 clean.py prices.csv
```

Running a script fits the same shape.
screens.question: In `python3 clean.py prices.csv`, which word is the command?

options.why: clean.py is a file. python3 is the program that reads it and runs it, so clean.py is an argument.
prices.csv is a second argument, which python3 hands on to the script.

hints.text: Which word comes first?
The first word is always the command. Everything after it is options and arguments.

feedback.correct: python3 is the command; the script is its argument.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The command is always the first word.

explain.text: python3 is the program; clean.py tells it which script to run. prices.csv is passed on for the script to read. You will write and run such a script in the next level.

screens.prose: Your broker drops a trade export into ~/exports each evening. A script needs the name of the newest one. You are in ~/exports. Note that `head -1` is short for `head -n 1`.
screens.question: Build the command that prints only the newest file's name.

hints.text: First list newest first, then keep one line.
This is the file you want printed.
`ls -t` lists newest first; a pipe hands that to `head -1`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List newest first, then pass the list to head.

byKey.r: -r flips the order, so the oldest export comes first. head -1 would print trades_0301.csv.
byKey.gt: `>` would write the list into a file named head. A pipe passes it to the head command.

explain.text: ls -t ranks the files newest first, and head -1 keeps the top line. The pipeline prints trades_0305.csv. Tomorrow it prints tomorrow's file, with no editing.

ideas: Options start with a dash and change how a command behaves; arguments say what it works on.
`man` and `--help` list a command's options. Read them before guessing.
Running a script is a command too: `python3 script.py`, with the script as its argument.

formula.name: Shape of a command line
formula.note: For example `head -n 3 prices.csv`. Single letters can share one dash: `ls -lt`.

summary.trap: A letter means what each command says it means. `-r` is reverse for sort but recursive for rm.

quiz.prose:
In grep, `-i` means ignore case. prices.csv holds three AAPL lines, all in capitals.

```sh
$ grep -i aapl prices.csv
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: Without -i that would be right. With it, aapl matches AAPL.
-i changes how letters compare, not which lines count. Only lines with aapl in any case match.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what -i changes.

explain.text: -i makes grep treat capitals and small letters as the same. So aapl finds the three AAPL lines.

quiz.prose: You want the full list of grep's options.
quiz.question: Which command shows it?

options.why: That runs grep, searching for the text man. It waits for input instead of showing help.
Guessing an option gives an error. The manual lists the real ones.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which command opens a manual page?

explain.text: man grep opens grep's manual page. Space scrolls, / searches, and q quits.

quiz.prose:
dates.txt holds three dates, one per line: 2024-03-01, 2024-03-05, 2024-03-04.

```sh
$ sort -r dates.txt | head -1
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You dropped the -r. Reversed, the latest date comes first.
That is the last line of the file. sort reorders lines before head sees them.

feedback.correct: Reversed, the latest date comes first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sort the dates, flip them, then keep the first.

explain.text: Year-month-day dates sort correctly as text. -r puts the latest first, and head -1 keeps it: 2024-03-05.

quiz.prose: `ls -a` lists all names, including hidden ones that start with a dot. A folder holds .env, data and notes.txt.
quiz.question: How many names does `ls -a` print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Remember the two hidden names every folder has.

byKey.three: You counted .env, data and notes.txt. ls -a also lists . and .., the folder itself and its parent.
byKey.visible: That is plain ls. -a adds the hidden names.

explain.text: Every folder holds two hidden entries: . for itself and .. for its parent. With .env, data and notes.txt, ls -a prints 5 names.
